node.label: Partha Chatterjee
node.date_label: 1986 Nationalist Thought and the Colonial World · 1993 The Nation and Its Fragments · 2012 The Black Hole of Empire
node.description: Partha Chatterjee studies colonial nationalism and the changing practices of imperial power. His work joins political theory and anthropology to historical research on colonial and postcolonial India. In his interview about The Black Hole of Empire, he explains how a local story of Calcutta and its memorial becomes the spine of a wider inquiry into concepts and practices of empire. He also identifies a lesson from Subaltern Studies: popular cultural forms can be analysed alongside elite political discourse. These are selective historical methods rather than a claim that one account exhausts empire.

proposed_edges.relationship: Braids a local imperial narrative with the history of governing concepts and practices
proposed_edges.evidence_note: The 2012 interview at 2–3 explains how Fort William and the Black Hole story connect with selectively traced political economy, law and techniques of imperial power. Chatterjee explicitly notes that selection was necessary; no exhaustive global history is inferred.

proposed_edges.relationship: Brings popular cultural practices into the historical analysis of imperial power
proposed_edges.evidence_note: At 2, Chatterjee says he learned through Subaltern Studies to interrogate popular culture theoretically. Theatre and football enter alongside policy and elite discourse. His sweeping claim about what other intellectual historians omit is not adopted.
